Container.Name: ArrowLoop
Container.Overview:
Two-way file synchronisation that shows you the plan before it moves anything.
Every other sync tool's main screen is a progress bar, which is a report on a decision somebody already made for you. Here you get the decision: every proposed change listed with its direction and the reason for it, each row unticked if you disagree, and nothing touched until you press the button.
It keeps a per-file record of what both sides looked like the last time they agreed, which is what lets it tell "created over here" apart from "deleted over there" instead of guessing. Deletions go to a trash rather than away. A run that would delete an implausible share of your files stops and says so. A side that lists nothing at all is never believed, because a disk that failed to mount looks exactly like a folder somebody emptied.
Local folders, Unraid shares, SMB, SFTP and S3-compatible storage, with rclone compiled in rather than shelled out to.
Note: the WebUI has no login of its own. Keep it on your LAN or put it behind a reverse proxy that asks who you are.
Container.DonateText: If this template helps you, consider buying me a coffee.

Config.Name: WebUI Port
Config.Description: The port the interface listens on. It has no login of its own, so do not forward it from the internet.

Config.Name: Config
Config.Description: Holds arrowloop.json, one state database per job and the run log. This is the directory that must survive the container: without the state databases every job forgets what the two sides agreed on and treats every file as new.

Config.Name: Data
Config.Description: The shares you want to synchronise. Point job paths at subfolders of this, for example /data/Photos. Mount it read-write: a two-way job writes to both sides by definition.

Config.Name: Timezone
Config.Description: Used for the schedules. A cron expression means nothing until the container agrees with you about what time it is.

Config.Name: Listen address
Config.Description: Where the interface binds inside the container. Leave this alone unless you know why you are changing it: outside a container the program deliberately defaults to loopback, and the container overrides that because loopback inside a container means nobody can reach it.
